newsitem.title: PERU: Uruguayan ambassador released by Peruvian rebels.
newsitem.headline: Uruguayan ambassador released by Peruvian rebels.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence released Uruguay's ambassador on Tuesday after a Uruguayan court denied a Peruvian extradition request and freed two of their comrades.
Chief Red Cross negotiator Michel Minnig said Tabare Bocalandro's release reduced to 105 the number of hostages still being held by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
The two men walked slowly out of the residence side-by-side in a surprise twist to the hostage crisis.
Bocalandro, his head bowed and still dressed in the elegant suit he wore to the diplomatic reception that was stormed by guerrillas a week ago, was taken away in a police car.

Earlier on Tuesday, a Uruguayan appeals court ruled that Luis Alberto Samaniego and Silvia Gora Rivera, alleged MRTA members held in connection with the kidnapping of a Bolivian businessman, should not be extradited to Peru and ordered their release.
The ruling revoked a court decision in March to authorise Peru's request for the extradition of the couple.
Uruguayan officials insisted that it did not negotiate a swap and the two events were not connected.
"There were no negotiations. This is just a coincidence," Foreign Minister Alvaro Ramos told reporters in Montevideo.
"The court ruling was due in the case of the Peruvians, and proceedings finished today," he said.

But a well-placed government source said a deal had been cut with the MRTA guerrillas, who had not released the Uruguayan ambassador along with other diplomats on Sunday. "This was an exchange," the senior government aide told Reuters.

Samaniego and Gora were suspected of taken part in the 1995 kidnapping of Bolivian businessman and former government official, Samuel Doria Medina, who was freed a month and a half later after a $1.2 million ransom was paid.
Samaniego said the court's decision had come as a surprise.
"Since May the court had done nothing," he told Uruguay's Channel Four television network. "We still don't know if our freedom is unconditional or...if they could arrest us again."
It was the first release from the besieged residence since 225 men were freed on Sunday night and briefly brightened an otherwise cheerless Christmas Eve for the hostages.

The rebels who stormed the elegant cocktail party at the ambassador's residence still hold six foreign ambassadors, two Peruvian government ministers, dozens of Japanese businessmen and the brother of Peru's President Alberto Fujimori.
